analysis.one_liner: Doubles the federal cigarette tax and raises taxes on cigars, chewing tobacco, and nicotine pouches to match it.
analysis.headline: The Tobacco Tax Equity Act never got a committee vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from April 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would roughly double the federal cigarette tax (from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand cigarettes) and bring cigars, pipe tobacco, chewing tobacco, nicotine pouches, and other nicotine products up to the same per-use tax rate as cigarettes, with rates rising with inflation afterward. Higher prices are the main tool for cutting smoking, especially among young people, and the tax raises federal revenue. But tobacco taxes fall hardest on low-income smokers, who smoke at higher rates and would pay the increase directly at the register.
analysis.who_benefits: People who don't use tobacco gain from lower smoking rates and secondhand smoke exposure, particularly young people, who are the most price-sensitive group. Federal and state governments gain revenue. Smokers who quit or never start gain the largest health benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Non-smokers, young people, and government revenue

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the federal cigarette excise tax from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand, adding roughly $1 to the price of a pack [S3].

Ends the large gaps that let some products be taxed far below cigarettes: chewing tobacco would jump from $1.51 to $26.84 per pound, small cigars and roll-your-own tobacco would match the cigarette rate, and large cigars would move from a percentage tax to a per-pound rate [S3].
Taxing all nicotine products at a cigarette-equivalent per-use rate closes the pricing gap that has made pouches, lozenges, and vape products cheap alternatives for young users [S3].
Rates would rise automatically with inflation each year, so the health and revenue effects would not erode over time [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill simply as raising the cigarette excise tax and equalizing rates among all other tobacco products [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco and nicotine users pay the tax directly, and because smoking is concentrated among lower-income households, the burden is regressive. Tobacco manufacturers, vape and nicotine-pouch makers, and retailers lose sales, and retailers holding inventory when rates rise would owe a one-time tax on that stock (with a $500 credit).
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokers, vape users, and tobacco retailers

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on tobacco are regressive: lower-income smokers spend a larger share of their income on the tax and would pay roughly $1 more per pack, whether or not they cut back [S3].

Retailers and distributors holding untaxed inventory when the rate rises would owe a floor-stocks tax on that stock within 120 days, a cash burden that falls hardest on small shops, though each person gets a $500 credit [S3].

Raising prices sharply on some products but not on untaxed illicit or unregulated alternatives can push some users toward black-market cigarettes, which are not collected or controlled by any regulator.
Higher taxes cut sales, so manufacturers, distributors, and vape shops bear reduced revenue on top of the tax itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is real: price is one of the most effective levers for reducing smoking, especially for teenagers, and equalizing rates would close loopholes that keep cheap nicotine products on shelves. But the cost is paid almost entirely by users, skewing toward low-income households, and there is no offsetting benefit like a rebate or refundable credit for them. It is a genuine public-health measure with a genuinely regressive price tag, and an honest supporter has to weigh both.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) introduced the Tobacco Tax Equity Act of 2021 on April 22, 2021, joined by eight Democratic senators (Wyden, Murray, Brown, Reed, Merkley, Blumenthal, Markey, and Hirono) [S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action it ever received [S5].
No Republican signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no bipartisan base to help it move [S4].
The Finance Committee never scheduled the bill for consideration, and it expired at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023 without a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco and nicotine manufacturers came out ahead: cigarette, cigar, chewing-tobacco, and vape producers kept the current low tax structure intact for another two years, and retailers avoided the one-time tax on existing inventory. Smokers also kept paying today's prices rather than the higher ones the bill would have charged, though they kept the health risks that came with them.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never moved far enough for a roll call to show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: Their products would face doubled or far higher excise taxes, cutting sales. Higher prices mean less smoking, so the industry's financial interest runs against the public-health purpose of the bill.

The bill taxes any nicotine product the FDA has determined to be a tobacco product at a cigarette-equivalent per-use rate, ending the low-price advantage that pouches, lozenges, and vape products have had. These products are heavily used by young people, so the industry's pricing interest runs against the bill's goal of discouraging youth nicotine use.

They would owe a one-time tax on inventory held when rates rise, payable within 120 days, with a $500 credit per person. This is a compliance and cash burden on top of reduced sales from higher prices.
